name: Height-stretching devices / inversion
lead: Height-stretching devices are products used or marketed to add height by stretching or decompressing the spine. The best-known are inversion tables and gravity boots, which hang a person by the ankles at an inverted angle so that body weight pulls the vertebrae apart, a form of gravity-assisted spinal traction [1]. People in height-focused communities use them to recover or hold the extra centimetre or so of stature that the spine carries in the morning, when the discs are fully hydrated and unloaded, and some hope to extend that effect over months [2][3][9].

The mechanism people point to is real physiology: the spinal column is a stack of fluid-filled discs, and a person is measurably taller after lying down than after a day of standing and exercise [9]. Traction and inversion are intended to widen the spaces between vertebrae for the duration of the session [1][11]. Reference sources describe the effect as temporary, with short-term elongation that largely reverses within about an hour of standing [4], and an inversion session is usually described as lasting about ten minutes or less [1].

Research on inversion and related traction has mostly examined back pain rather than stature. Reviews of mechanical traction report short-term pain relief in some conditions, while a Cochrane review of traction for low-back pain reported low-to-moderate quality evidence of no clinically significant benefit [4][11][10]. Documented risks include raised heart rate, raised pressure inside the eye, acid reflux and ankle strain, with higher risk for people with cardiac disease, hypertension, glaucoma or pregnancy [1][4]. Permanent height gain from limb-lengthening surgery is a separate, surgical practice [13].

chain: Hanging inverted or in traction separates the vertebrae

angle.text: People use inversion tables, gravity boots and traction devices to decompress the spine, aiming to measure at their fullest morning height or to hold that height later in the day. Reference sources describe the gain as millimetres to a few centimetres of temporary spinal elongation rather than a change in bone length.

paras: Inversion therapy involves hanging by the legs, ankles or feet at an inverted angle, up to fully upside down [1]. Equipment falls into a few families. Inversion tables are frames with ankle clamps that tilt the user back through a range of angles, with Grokipedia describing steel frames rated for roughly 250 to 350 pounds and angles of about 20 to 90 degrees [4]. Gravity boots are padded ankle cuffs that hook onto a doorway or pull-up bar [1][4]. Inversion chairs are seated variants for users with limited mobility [4]. Wikipedia's traction article groups inversion with other non-bony 'spinal decompression' methods, alongside inflatable girdles, flexed-hip chairs and hanging from the arms in pull-ups or chin-ups [11].

Clinical mechanical traction, which physiotherapists apply with a motorised table and harness, is the medical relative of these home devices. Wikipedia describes it as used for cervical and lumbar disorders such as radiculopathy and spinal stenosis, delivered continuously or intermittently [11].

sections.h: How people use them for height
paras: In height-focused communities, the stated aim is usually modest and timing-related rather than permanent growth. A thread on looksmax.org cites a person said to have gone from 5'10 to 6'0 in ten days of table use, with the original poster noting the gain was in morning height only and faded by evening [2]. Others in the same threads describe the gain as decompression of the spine rather than growth [3].

Because stature varies through the day, the reasoning has a physical basis. Wikipedia's human height article cites a study of 100 children who lost a mean of 1.54 cm between getting out of bed and mid-afternoon, and notes that exercise shortly before measuring can lower height while lying down for a long period can raise it [9]. Wikipedia also notes that a typical measurement error of about 0.5 cm can mask true small changes [9]. The same article attributes lifelong shrinkage of stature in older age partly to loss of disc height through desiccation [9].

Some posters pair table use with joint supplements, hoping to retain the gain, and others discuss saving for limb-lengthening surgery instead, describing table results as lost through the day [2][3]. Wikipedia describes cosmetic limb lengthening as an established but high-complication surgery with reported infection rates of about 5 percent, which is a separate and much larger intervention [13].

Grokipedia traces inverted postures to Indian yoga and Ayurvedic traditions, citing the Hatha Yoga Pradipika (15th century) and its description of Viparita Karani, and reports that Hippocrates, around 400 BCE, reportedly suspended patients upside down, with Galen refining the method and Vidus Vidius illustrating it in the 16th century [4]. Wikipedia's traction article independently shows an early Greek traction device from a Byzantine edition of Galen's work [11].

The modern consumer products are credited to Dr. Robert Martin, a California osteopath, chiropractor and physician, who developed the first modern inversion table in the 1960s as part of a 'Gravity Guidance System' and whose gravity boots were patented in the 1970s through Gravity Guidance Inc. [4]. Roger Teeter founded Teeter Corporation in 1981 after personal back pain, later selling tables and boots under the Hang Ups brand; Grokipedia reports industry sales above $70 million by 1982, a 1980 appearance of the devices in the film American Gigolo, and FDA 510(k) clearances as Class I devices in the 1990s [4]. Wikipedia cites a 1983 Time article on gravity boots in workouts [1]. Grokipedia also reports that the US Army Physical Fitness School adopted inversion for training and rehabilitation in 1998 [4]. These details come from an AI-generated encyclopedia and are attributed to it.

Wikipedia explains that body weight acting in the inverted position creates a distracting force that slightly and temporarily increases the spacing between vertebrae, which may reduce pressure on nerve roots and relax muscles, in the same way as clinical traction [1]. Grokipedia states that the effect is mostly short-term and reverses after sessions [4].

Wikipedia's article on traction reports three 2017 studies in which traction increased nutrient and water flow into intervertebral discs, which is part of the rationale people give for combining stretching with disc health [11]. The same article notes that inconsistent traction protocols may explain mixed findings and that force, rhythm, duration and frequency need further study [11]. Grokipedia adds that one radiographic study reported separation across the lumbar segments that totalled about 2.9 cm at moderate angles after 5 to 10 minutes, and separately describes whole-body stature gains of about 5 to 9 mm that largely reverse within an hour [4]. Its radiographic figures describe segment spacing, not a change in measured stature, and they come from an unverified source.

A comparison people sometimes raise is spaceflight, where Wikipedia reports that astronauts' height increases by about 2.5 cm within one month as the skeleton extends in weightlessness [12]. The article does not describe the timeline of reversal after return, and it ties the change to sustained removal of gravity loading, not a brief session [12].

Wikipedia describes inversion as a form of spinal traction that may briefly relieve pain, with its main reported benefit a pleasant sensation within minutes, and it cites 2021 material stating that most people do not recover faster or better with it [1]. Its disc herniation article says non-surgical spinal decompression has very limited supporting evidence and has had controversial marketing [5], and its spinal decompression article cites a 2007 paper asking whether the literature supports advertising claims for non-surgical decompression [10]. A 2023 article in Disability and Rehabilitation offers recommendations for inversion table therapy [6].

Grokipedia lists several studies. Gianakopoulos and colleagues (1985) reported radiographic lumbar distraction of several millimetres at L3-L4 and L4-L5 with no short-term cardiovascular harm; Vernon and colleagues (1985) reported reduced paraspinal electromyographic activity and 1 to 2 mm of distraction at L4-S1 in healthy volunteers; Prasad and colleagues (2012) ran a randomised pilot of 24 patients awaiting discectomy and found no significant difference in pain or disability, with surgery avoided in 77 percent of the inversion group versus 22 percent of controls at six months; and Alrwaily and colleagues (2021) followed 85 patients with disc protrusions and sciatica through a three-week protocol and reported improved pain and disability scores [4]. Grokipedia also cites a Cochrane review of 32 randomised trials with 2,762 participants that found low-to-moderate quality evidence of no clinically significant benefit of traction for low-back pain, noting small samples, risk of bias and possible industry funding [4].

Wikipedia's article on spinal decompression reports that mechanical traction was superior to conventional physical therapy in the short term but not in all studies beyond six months, and a 2020 review cited there found mechanical traction outperformed manual traction [10][11].

Wikipedia states that inversion raises heart rate, cardiac output, peripheral resistance, venous return and myocardial oxygen consumption, citing a 1992 study in the International Journal of Sports Medicine, and lists people with heart disease, high blood pressure or eye disease such as glaucoma, and pregnant people, as higher-risk groups [1]. It also notes that acid reflux with an inversion table can be painful and nauseating, that most people find the ankles uncomfortable after a few minutes, that sessions should be short, with 10 minutes the cited maximum, and that new users may need help getting out of the apparatus [1].

Grokipedia reports intraocular pressure rising from about 16.8 mmHg seated to about 32.9 mmHg after five minutes inverted in one cited set of figures, as well as a case of bilateral retinal detachment in a 67-year-old after seven years of intermittent use, dizziness on standing, falls from equipment failure, ankle strain and isolated subconjunctival haemorrhage [4]. It lists contraindications including uncontrolled hypertension, recent stroke, glaucoma, retinal detachment, cerebral aneurysm, recent spinal surgery, hiatal hernia and osteoporosis [4].

No studies found testing inversion tables or stretching devices for lasting height increase in healthy people. Studies of related traction and inversion have examined pain and function. A registered trial compares inversion table therapy with manual therapy for pain and lumbar flexibility in chronic low back pain (NCT07055802, started March 2025, 54 participants) [7]. A randomised trial of a high-intensity home stretching device examined adhesive capsulitis of the shoulder, which does not address stature [8]. Grokipedia also cites an eight-week trial at a steep inverted angle that reported improved trunk flexion and extension [4].

Height-focused communities discuss several overlapping methods: hanging from a bar, spinal-decompression stretches, posture work, sleep and measurement-timing habits, and, at the far end, limb-lengthening surgery. Wikipedia describes surgical lengthening as proposed by Bernhard von Langenbeck in 1869, first attempted clinically by Alessandro Codivilla in 1905, and made widely usable by Gavriil Ilizarov from the 1950s; it reports that China's Ministry of Health banned the operation in 2006 after serious side effects and that demand in India is high [13].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, inversion tables are debated as a height tool, usually in terms of temporary morning height rather than permanent growth, and are often set against limb-lengthening as the only route to lasting height.[2][3]

claims.claim: An inversion table can add about two inches of morning height.
claims.believers: One poster cites a person said to have gone from 5'10 to 6'0 in 10 days, noting the gain was in morning height only and wearing off by evening.[2]
claims.experts: Grokipedia reports short-term elongation of millimetres that largely reverses within about an hour, and Wikipedia's inversion page does not address height.[4][1]

claims.claim: Glucosamine could help keep the height gained from inversion.
claims.believers: The original poster says he is considering glucosamine sulphate to retain morning gains, and another reply says it is better to use glucosamine than a table.[2][3]
claims.experts: No published study located has tested glucosamine for retaining height from inversion.

claims.claim: Inversion only decompresses the spine and is a cope.
claims.believers: Some posters say gains disappear during the day and advise saving money for limb lengthening; another says it only decompresses the spine.[2][3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia and Grokipedia describe the effect as temporary spinal spacing and short-lived.[1][4]

claims.claim: Using the table for months or years could make the gain last.
claims.believers: The original poster argues that a ten-day trial was too short and that months or years of use, with supplements, might hold the gain.[2]
claims.experts: No published study located has followed healthy adults using inversion for stature over months or years; Wikipedia attributes lifelong height loss partly to disc desiccation.[9]

claims.claim: Measuring height first thing in the morning gives the true maximum, so decompression before a measurement helps.
claims.believers: Posters discussing morning height treat the unloaded spine as the tallest state and look for ways to reach it on demand.[2]
claims.experts: Wikipedia cites a study of 100 children with a mean fall of 1.54 cm from morning to mid-afternoon, and notes that lying down for long periods can raise measured height.[9]

claims.claim: Inversion is safe for anyone as a casual stretch.
claims.believers: Proponents of casual use point to short sessions of about ten minutes or less, which Wikipedia notes usually feel pleasant within a few minutes.[1]
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists higher risk for people with heart disease, hypertension, glaucoma or pregnancy, and Grokipedia reports raised eye pressure and rare retinal detachment.[1][4]

card.summary: Inversion tables and stretch devices for height; any gain reported is millimetres and short-lived.
card.note: Cardiac, eye-pressure and fall risks are documented for inversion.

quick.overview:
Inversion tables and gravity boots hang a person at an inverted angle to decompress the spine. Forum users discuss them as a way to gain morning height.

Reference sources describe short-term spinal elongation that reverses within about an hour and no strong evidence of lasting height gain in adults.
quick.mechanism: Gravity-assisted traction briefly increases spacing between vertebrae, which is the basis of the claimed height effect.
quick.risks: Wikipedia lists raised heart rate and cardiac workload, acid reflux and ankle discomfort, with higher risk for people with heart disease, hypertension, glaucoma or pregnancy. Grokipedia adds eye pressure and fall injuries.
